title: Principle and Foundation
hookLine: we are made to praise, reverence and serve God

lines: ASKED AT BEDTIME AND AT 3 A.M.
cards: Why am I here? A child can ask it at bedtime. A teenager, slamming a door.

A grown-up at three in the morning, or in a hospital corridor, or on the drive home from a job they don't love. It's an easy question to leave unanswered while the dishes wait. Ignatius doesn't leave it.

Before the retreat's first week, before a single meditation on sin or mercy or the life of Christ, he sets one short paragraph at the door. It answers that question in a sentence, and everything after is built on top.

teach.b: Ignatius calls it the Principle and Foundation, and it begins with the human person. In his words, put plainly: we are created to praise, to reverence, and to serve God our Lord, and by doing this to save our souls.

Praise is the mouth: noticing and saying that something is good. Reverence is the posture: treating God, and the world God made, with care, not carelessness. Serve is the hands: doing something about it.
Then the second move, and it's practical.
Everything else on the face of the earth, Ignatius says, is created to help us toward that purpose. So things are tools, not goals.
A career, a house, a reputation, even health: each is good to the degree it helps, and a problem to the degree it gets in the way. Tomorrow stays with what that asks.
For today, notice the order: purpose first, then everything else measured against it.
The book of Ecclesiastes, after a long search through pleasure and work and wisdom, comes to rest in a similar place, in the Douay-Rheims: "Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is all man."
The whole of a person, in one line. A foundation is the part of a house nobody admires and everybody stands on. Get the bottom right, the paragraph suggests, and the rest of the building can go up.

how: Retreat directors give the Principle and Foundation to retreatants at the start of the Spiritual Exercises, and Jesuit schools and retreat programs return to it as a short statement of what a human life is for.

o: the cornerstone of the first Jesuit church
Ignatius's opening words on why we're made
the first rule in the Jesuit order's charter

p: the mouth: saying it is good
tools to help toward the purpose

s: the Principle and Foundation comes at the end of the Exercises

for Ignatius, things like health and reputation are goals in themselves

games.q: you're Ignatius, about to open a month-long retreat. what do you put at the very start?
o: one short paragraph on what a person is made for.
a schedule of the day's prayers.
games.why: before the first week, he sets the Principle and Foundation: we are created to praise, reverence and serve God, and everything else is to help.

practice: On a scrap of paper or your phone, write one sentence that begins: I am here to.
It can borrow Ignatius's three verbs, praise, reverence, serve, or be in your own words, to love my kids well, to make things, to tell the truth; read it back once, slowly.
If you pray, hold the sentence up to God and leave it there.

wordCard.voice: Principle and Foundation. Ignatius's opening paragraph of the Exercises: we're made to praise, reverence and serve God, and everything else is meant to help. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: made for this. Purpose first, then everything else. Back tomorrow, same hill.
